name: Stimmung
editorial_article: *Stimmung* (1968) is a seminal work of 20th-century avant-garde music by German composer Karlheinz Stockhausen, written for six vocalists and six microphones. Commissioned by the City of Cologne for the Collegium Vocale Köln, the piece stands as a milestone in Western composition for being the first major work based entirely on the production of vocal harmonics and overtones. Spanning approximately 74 minutes, *Stimmung* utilizes a low B♭1 drone—inaudible to the audience—as the fundamental frequency from which the singers expand into a series of vocal overtone models. The title itself, *Stimmung*, is a rich German term that encapsulates "tuning"—not only in the musical sense, but also referring to the tuning of the soul and the psychological resonance between performers.\n\nThe piece is structured into 51 "moments" using what Stockhausen defined as "moment form," where the sequence of pitches is fixed, but the specific distribution of rhythmic models, phonetic patterns, and lyrical elements remains within the discretion of the performers. The vocalists incorporate diverse materials, including "magic names" of various global deities and erotic love poetry written by the composer. Inspired by his experiences in Mexico and his time spent in Madison, Connecticut, Stockhausen discovered the technique of overtone singing through his young son. By grounding the composition in just intonation, *Stimmung* creates a hypnotic, meditative space that challenges traditional Western harmonic structures, acting as a bridge between serialism and the meditative, drone-based explorations emerging in the avant-garde of the era. It remains a testament to Stockhausen's ability to synthesize rigid structural organization with deep, visceral sonic exploration, and has been performed by numerous specialized ensembles, including Theatre of Voices and Singcircle, over the decades since its inception.
